title: Dile que venga
blurbEn: Asking people to do things at work, where the subjunctive does most of its everyday work.
body:
Mi jefe quiere que organice la reunión del viernes.

Me ha pedido que llame a los clientes, que reserve una sala y que prepare los documentos antes del jueves.

También quiere que Diego venga, aunque Diego odia las reuniones.

—Dile que venga —me dice mi jefe.

—Dile tú —pienso, pero no lo digo.

Al final le escribo un mensaje: «Diego, el jefe pide que estés el viernes a las diez. Lo siento».

Contesta en dos segundos: «Dile que tengo una cita con el dentista».

No tiene ninguna cita. Los dos lo sabemos. Es una excusa perfecta y yo nunca me atrevo a inventarme una.

Pero le admiro un poco.
translationEn:
My boss wants me to organise Friday's meeting.

He has asked me to call the clients, book a room and prepare the documents before Thursday.

He also wants Diego to come, although Diego hates meetings.

"Tell him to come," my boss says.

"You tell him," I think, but I don't say it.

In the end I write him a message: "Diego, the boss is asking you to be here on Friday at ten. Sorry."

He replies in two seconds: "Tell him I have a dentist's appointment."

He doesn't have any appointment. We both know it. It's a perfect excuse and I never dare invent one.

But I admire him a little.

organice.note: The z becomes c before e. A spelling change, not a grammar one.

Dile que venga.note: 'decir que' + subjunctive is an instruction. With the indicative — 'dile que viene' — it would report a fact: tell him that he is coming.

phrases.gloss: He has asked me to call
phrases.note: 'pedir que' always takes the subjunctive — asking is wanting by another name.
